analysis.title: Community Board Seats Call for Feedback

chapters.title: Trustee Evaluation Form and Rubric Usage
chapters.summary: Andrew asks how the board evaluation rubric is applied and whether it creates an intimidating barrier for community candidates.

chapters.title: Board Professionalization and Quotas
chapters.summary: Participants debate whether the rubric drives an overly corporate board and discuss the utility of quotas versus skill requirements.

chapters.title: Affiliate Perspective and Organizational Scale
chapters.summary: Speaker F shares local chapter election experiences, while Christophe highlights the governance demands of a large-scale global NGO.

chapters.title: Fiduciary Duties to Foundation versus Movement
chapters.summary: A debate emerges over whether trustees are legally bound strictly to the Wikimedia Foundation entity or to the wider movement.

chapters.title: Governance Expectations and Communication Gaps
chapters.summary: The discussion examines regional differences in board perception, trustee time commitments, and the need for clearer governance communication.

chapters.title: Leadership Development and Historical Shifts
chapters.summary: Participants consider board leadership training at conferences and trace the root of fiduciary tensions to the 2011 Haifa decision.

actionItems.text: Include community feedback regarding quotas and board selection into the consultation report.

insights.text: The Board approved the trustee evaluation rubric by a 9 to 1 vote prior to defining its specific implementation details.
How the trustee evaluation rubric will be operationalized within the different proposed board seat selection pathways remains undefined.
The trustee evaluation form does not have a preset minimum passing threshold but is intended to illustrate the range of qualifications sought for the board.
Trustees possess a legal fiduciary duty specifically to the Wikimedia Foundation rather than to the wider movement or individual affiliates.
Fiduciary obligations to the corporate entity can fundamentally conflict with movement-wide desires when making global organizational decisions.
Much of the community assumes board members act as stewards for the broader movement rather than corporate directors of a specific non-profit entity.
Participants consistently request structured training programs to build community governance skills and prepare volunteers for board leadership.
The 2011 Haifa resolution restricting affiliate fundraising marked the pivotal shift where the board distinctly prioritized corporate protection over movement consensus.
